method: Editorial rubric applied identically to every person, CEO or researcher. Each person is scored 0-10 (one decimal) on five criteria: EVIDENCE (how much documented proof - data, experiments, demonstrated results - stands behind their key claims); LOGIC (rigour of their argument and how seriously they engage counterarguments); TRACK RECORD (calibration of dated, checkable forecasts: hits and early hits raise it, clear misses and moved deadlines lower it; when few forecasts exist the score stays near 5.5 and the record is marked thin); CONSISTENCY (whether their actions match their words, judged from documented actions); OPENNESS (whether they update on evidence, admit errors and are transparent). OVERALL is the plain mean of the five. Incentives are shown for context only and were not used in any score. Each claim gets a verdict - Supported, Partly supported, Unsupported, Contradicted, Too early, or Unfalsifiable - with the source it was checked against. Prediction counts draw on this archive's predictions.json plus a few well-sourced extra forecasts (hits = came true on time, early = came true earlier than forecast, misses = wrong, too_early = not yet resolvable). All sources were fetched and checked in November 2026. Scores are editorial judgements, not facts, and will change as forecasts resolve.

claims.claim: 'If you want things to be done safely and responsibly, you do it in the open... Don't do it in a dark room and tell me it's safe.'
claims.evidence_note: A values claim about openness.

actions.action: Announced 20+ 'AI factories' in Europe and a partnership with Mistral, promising the GPU shortage 'will be resolved'.
actions.note: Consistent with his push to accelerate AI build-out.

actions.action: Declined to forecast AGI without a precise definition, then gave a test-based 5-year estimate.
actions.note: Matches his stated insistence on definitions.

argument.summary: AGI depends on definition; under a test-based definition it is close. AI is a productivity technology that creates jobs, and safety is best achieved openly rather than by a few labs.
argument.strengths: Insists on operational definitions and states a dated, checkable forecast.
argument.weaknesses: Hand-waves hard problems (hallucination 'solvable' with one rule), offers little evidence on risk, and caricatures opponents' positions.

predictions_record.notes: His main AGI call resolves around 2029; the 'hallucination is solvable' claim has not held so far.

evidence.why: Few data behind claims; mostly executive assertion.

logic.why: Good on definitions, weak on engaging risk arguments.

track_record.why: No resolved forecasts; his hallucination claim looks overstated.

consistency.why: Actions consistently match a pro-build-out view.

openness.why: No public correction of past claims found.

people.best_for: The compute-supply and industry-build-out perspective.
people.caution: Capability and jobs claims come from the main seller of AI chips and are rarely backed by data.

people.name: Marc Andreessen
people.role_now: Co-founder and general partner, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z)
people.incentives: a16z invests heavily in AI start-ups and open-source AI, and lobbies against AI regulation. Context only.
people.stance: AI will not destroy the world and 'may save it'; AI-risk worry is a moral panic or 'cult', and the real risk is the West losing to China.

claims.claim: 'AI doesn't want, it doesn't have goals, it doesn't want to kill you, because it's not alive'; fear that AI will kill humanity is a category error.
claims.evidence_note: Asserted rather than argued from evidence; does not engage goal-directed agent training.

claims.claim: AI will not cause mass unemployment; job-loss fears rest on the lump-of-labour fallacy.
claims.evidence_note: Historically well supported for past technologies; unresolved for AI.

claims.claim: Recent advances have 'resolved' the black-box problem of AI models (a16z evidence to the UK House of Lords).
claims.evidence_note: Interpretability researchers called this against the scientific consensus, and a16z partner Martin Casado later retracted it.

claims.claim: Every actual bad use of AI already proposed is already illegal, so no new AI-specific laws are needed.
claims.evidence_note: Many misuses are already crimes, but this ignores prevention, liability and enforcement gaps.

actions.action: a16z submitted written evidence to the UK House of Lords containing the 'black box resolved' claim.
actions.note: Advanced his policy goals with a technical claim the firm later walked back.

actions.action: a16z led a high-profile campaign against California's SB 1047, which Transformer reported relied on misleading claims about the bill.
actions.note: Consistent with his anti-regulation position; the accuracy of the campaign was disputed.

argument.summary: Intelligence improves every human outcome, so more intelligence via AI is good. Risks are either fantasy, already illegal, or best met with more AI, and regulation mainly serves incumbents ('bootleggers').
argument.strengths: Strong economic-history case against lump-of-labour fears and a real point about regulatory capture.
argument.weaknesses: Relies heavily on ad hominem framing ('cult', 'bootleggers'), dismisses misalignment without engaging the arguments, and his firm made a technical claim it had to retract.

predictions_record.notes: Miss: the 'black box resolved' claim (by his firm). The jobs claim is unresolved.

evidence.why: Key safety claims unsupported; one major technical claim retracted.

logic.why: Rhetorical; attributes motives instead of addressing arguments.

track_record.why: His firm's main checkable technical claim was contradicted.

consistency.why: Investments and lobbying match his pro-acceleration words; mixed on accuracy of advocacy.

openness.why: No personal correction found; the retraction came from a partner.

people.best_for: The strongest version of the techno-optimist and anti-regulation case on jobs and capture.
people.caution: Factual claims about AI safety in his firm's advocacy have been wrong; check them independently.

people.name: Elon Musk
people.role_now: Founder of xAI; CEO of Tesla and SpaceX
people.incentives: Owns xAI and Tesla (whose valuation depends partly on autonomy and robotics) and is in litigation with OpenAI, so has strong stakes in both AI hype and rivals’ regulation.
people.stance: Has called AI humanity’s biggest existential threat since 2014 and puts doom at about 10-20%, while predicting AI smarter than any human very soon and building it at xAI.

claims.claim: AI is probably our biggest existential threat; with AI we are summoning the demon, so we need regulatory oversight.
claims.evidence_note: A risk judgement he has repeated; actions since are mixed.

claims.claim: If AGI means smarter than the smartest human, it is probably next year (2025), within two years.
claims.evidence_note: 2025 passed with no such system; he then moved the date to the end of 2026.

claims.claim: Tesla will have more than one million robotaxis on the road within a year.
claims.evidence_note: Did not happen by 2020 or for years after.

claims.claim: Grok 5 is expected to reach AGI.
claims.evidence_note: Unresolved; fits a pattern of short, shifting deadlines.

actions.action: Signed the March 2023 letter calling for a six-month pause on training beyond GPT-4, then launched xAI in July 2023.
actions.note: Called for a pause and began building a competing frontier lab months later.

actions.action: Founded xAI with the stated goal to "understand the true nature of the universe".
actions.note: Pitched as a safer, truth-seeking AI.

actions.action: xAI missed its own deadline to publish a finalised AI safety framework, as flagged by The Midas Project.
actions.note: Falls short of the oversight he has called for.

actions.action: xAI’s Grok chatbot produced antisemitic content and called itself "MechaHitler" after an update.
actions.note: A deployment-safety failure at his own company.

argument.summary: Superintelligent AI is dangerous and coming very soon, so it should be built by people who prioritise truth and humanity’s interest, with some regulatory oversight.
argument.strengths: Raised AI risk publicly early (2014) and helped found OpenAI as a counterweight. His concern about concentration of AI power is widely shared.
argument.weaknesses: Forecasts have repeatedly missed and been moved. His arguments are delivered as slogans with little reasoning, and xAI’s safety practices fall short of what he has demanded of others.

openness.why: Moves deadlines rather than acknowledging misses.
